Every count, share and glucose value derived from those percentages in this lesson was computed here and is original. sources.license: US Government work; NIST states that information on its sites is public information and may be distributed or copied, with credit requested

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts that the binomial distribution is used when there are exactly two mutually exclusive outcomes of a trial, that it gives the probability of observing x successes in N trials with the probability of success on a single trial denoted p, that the distribution assumes p is fixed for all trials, that the probability mass function is n-choose-x times p to the x times (1 - p) to the (n - x), and that the mean is np and the standard deviation the square root of np(1 - p). The threshold, the value of p, the five-patient and sixty-patient worked examples, and every probability computed in this lesson are original. NIST copyright guidance at https://www.nist.gov/oism/copyrights states that NIST information is public information that may be distributed or copied and requests appropriate credit.

sources.publisher: European Mathematical Society and Springer, Encyclopedia of Mathematics
sources.version: Wiki entry retrieved 2026-07-25; adapted from an original article by L.N. Bol'shev in the Encyclopedia of Mathematics, ISBN 1402006098
sources.locator: Opening definition: the distribution of the number of positive results in a sequence of independent trials, with the stated probability formula, expectation np and variance np(1 - p)
sources.license: CC BY-SA 3.0 and GNU Free Documentation License, as stated on the encyclopedia's copyrights page

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the fact that the binomial distribution arises from a sequence of independent random variables each taking the value 1 with probability p and 0 with probability 1 - p, so that independence of trials is a condition of the model, together with the expectation np and variance np(1 - p) that corroborate the NIST record. The lesson's four-condition checklist, its independence counter-cases, and all wording are original.

sources.title: Bimodal distribution of glucose is not universally useful for diagnosing diabetes
sources.locator: Research Design and Methods, including the statistical methods paragraph on skewness and log transformation; Results and Conclusions of the structured abstract
sources.license: Copyright 2009 American Diabetes Association; the PMC record states readers may use the article under CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 for non-profit educational use with proper citation

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts that the DETECT-2 project pooled 43 studies covering 135,383 participants from 27 countries in which plasma glucose was measured during an oral glucose tolerance test; that the distributions of both fasting plasma glucose and 2-hour plasma glucose are skewed to the right; that glucose values were log transformed before model fitting to reduce that skew; that distributions of fasting and 2-hour plasma glucose did not in general produce bimodal structures useful for deriving cut points for diabetes; and that the presence of a biologically meaningful bimodal structure appeared to be driven by participants with known diabetes. No table, figure, dataset, wording or example from the article is reproduced, and the 1000-person screening dataset used in this lesson is constructed teaching material rather than any of the article's data.

sources.title: Glucose concentrations of less than 3.0 mmol/l (54 mg/dl) should be reported in clinical trials: a joint position statement of the American Diabetes Association and the European Association for the Study of Diabetes
sources.version: Diabetologia 2017 Jan;60(1):3-6, doi:10.1007/s00125-016-4146-6, PMID 27872948, PMCID PMC6518070; an erratum is recorded at Diabetologia 2017 Feb;60(2):377, doi:10.1007/s00125-016-4168-0
sources.locator: Title and body, at each point where a glucose concentration is reported in both mmol/l and mg/dl, including the glucose alert value of 3.9 mmol/l (70 mg/dl)
sources.license: Copyright the Author(s) 2016; distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License as stated on the article

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the paired reporting of glucose thresholds in both units, specifically 3.0 mmol/l as 54 mg/dl and the glucose alert value of 3.9 mmol/l as 70 mg/dl. Those pairings fix the conversion factor of 18 that this lesson uses to demonstrate that a z-score is unchanged by a unit conversion, and supply the alert value the constructed screening data are compared against. The lesson makes no recommendation about hypoglycaemia management or clinical trial reporting, and all wording, examples and arithmetic are original.
